content: Physical activity, including aerobic and resistance training, has been shown to improve health-related quality of life in individuals living with HIV. Recent studies indicate that engaging in aerobic exercise, progressive resistance training, or a combination of both leads to significant improvements in general health and mental health. Additionally, evidence suggests that both aerobic and multicomponent physical activities are associated with reductions in symptoms of depression and anxiety in people living with HIV. Research on the effects of physical activity on mental health symptoms has primarily focused on aerobic exercise, either alone or combined with progressive muscle-strengthening activities, as well as yoga. However, aerobic exercise alone or in combination with resistance training does not appear to significantly affect viral load or CD4 counts in individuals living with HIV. Direct evidence supports the inclusion of aerobic and muscle-strengthening physical activity in recommendations for individuals with type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Although there is limited published evidence, biological plausibility supports the benefits of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities for adults living with HIV and cancer survivors. Established international clinical practice guidelines, such as the ACSM Moving Through Cancer guidelines, also recommend these activities for these populations. However, the level of certainty in the evidence has been downgraded due to its emerging nature. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded the following: There is moderate certainty evidence supporting the combined or additive effects of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities in reducing cancer mortality and improving blood pressure in individuals with hypertension. High certainty evidence indicates that aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and combined activities improve markers of disease progression (e.g., HbA1c, blood pressure, BMI, and lipids) in adults with type 2 diabetes. Moderate certainty evidence suggests that regular aerobic exercise, alone or combined with resistance training, does not significantly alter viral load or CD4 counts in people living with HIV. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effects of strength training alone on health-related quality of life in individuals living with HIV. For adults and older adults with chronic conditions, including cancer survivors and those living with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and HIV, higher levels of sedentary behavior are associated with poor health outcomes, such as increased all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Recommendations for these populations include: Limiting sedentary time and replacing it with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activities, to gain health benefits. Engaging in more than the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity to counteract the negative effects of high sedentary behavior. For children and adolescents (aged 5–17 years) and adults (aged 18 years and older) living with disabilities, physical activity provides numerous health benefits. These include improved cognition in individuals with conditions affecting cognitive function (e.g., ADHD), enhanced physical function in children with intellectual disabilities, and improved quality of life. It is recommended that: Children and adolescents with disabilities engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily, primarily aerobic, across the week. Vigorous-intensity aerobic activities and muscleand bone-strengthening exercises should be included at least three days per week. Adults with disabilities perform at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination of both throughout the week. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week. Older adults with disabilities incorporate multicomponent physical activities emphasizing functional balance and strength training at least three days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. For individuals unable to meet these recommendations, doing some physical activity is better than none. Starting with small amounts of activity and gradually increasing frequency, intensity, and duration over time is encouraged. The health benefits of physical activity outweigh the risks when it is appropriate to an individual’s current activity level, health status, and physical function. The evidence supporting these recommendations was derived from comprehensive reviews of studies examining the associations between physical activity and health-related outcomes in individuals with disabilities resulting from conditions such as multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, intellectual disability, Parkinson’s disease, stroke, major clinical depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD. The outcomes examined included risk of comorbid conditions, physical function, cognitive function, and health-related quality of life.
